Issued at 317 PM EDT Wed Oct 14 2026

Surface cold frontal boundary has cleared southern portions of the 
forecast area this afternoon. The low level baroclinic zone is not 
expected to make much more additional southward progress into this 
evening as broad upper troughing across southern Ontario/Great 
Lakes region pushes east allowing some induced short wave upper 
ridging to build into the region downstream of larger scale cut-
off low. Some isolated showers are possible through late 
afternoon/early evening with weakening frontal zone across the 
south, but otherwise prospects for additional rainfall tonight 
look to be on the low side given southward frontal push and 
break in stronger short wave forcing.

Water vapor this imagery this afternoon depicts two features 
that will be watched over the next 48 hours including a cut-off 
upper level low across SW CO and a more progressive vort max 
spilling down eastern side of western Canadian upper trough. 
Present indications still suggest a phasing of these features 
Thursday evening across the Corn Belt and Upper Midwest. 
Isentropic progs of 300-305K layer do indicate a rapid uptick in
isentropic forcing toward late morning/midday. This evolution 
will allow the higher level theta-e air to return northward, 
particularly by Thursday evening. Showers with some embedded 
storms are expected to accompany this stronger advective push 
Thursday afternoon. Despite the strong advection, a strong low 
level inversion will develop in response and thus sensible 
warming at the surface likely to be more limited keeping highs 
in the 60s (possibly return of some low 70s late day/toward 
evening across the south). Severe weather is not expected during
the day Thursday given weak mid/upper level forcing outside of 
the strong advective forcing and due to the elevated nature of 
the instability.

For Thursday night, the aforementioned upstream facing should begin 
to induce cyclogenesis of associated low pressure, however some 
subtle but important trends in guidance have been noted. A 
subtle trend of slightly more positive tilt with the upper 
trough appears to be suggesting sfc low deepening rates will be 
a little less impressive and more delayed than earlier 
indications. Robust shear profiles will develop ahead of primary
low/sfc cold front but northward extent of a quality narrow 
warm sector remains uncertain, especially considering the trend 
of less rapid sfc feature deepening. There does still appear to 
be a narrow temporal window for weak near sfc instability across
the south depending on extent of warm frontal progression, but 
hi res ensemble means still support best surface-based and 
mixed-layer CAPE remaining across central/southern IN. Only 
minor changes were made to SWODY2 with a Marginal Risk of severe
storms persisting south of US 24, and mainly for the evening 
hours Thursday. Some isolated wind/tornado risk is possible 
where some weak MLCAPE can overspread given background low and 
deep layer shear, but current parameter space would tend to be 
more supportive of isolated severe threat southwest/south of 
local area from southern IL into central IN. Another limiting 
factor for severe potential could be more delayed impressive 
dynamics due to the weak positive tilt of this system. 
Otherwise, some brief locally heavy rain is possible with highly
anomalous 1.75+ inch PWATs working into the area ahead of the 
overnight cold frontal passage.

Friday still appears to be blustery/windy day with strong cold 
advection on the back side of this system. This should lead to 
development of lake effect rain showers and a potential of mixing 
down some stronger wind gusts. With deepening rates of this 
system perhaps a bit weaker than earlier indications and some 
suggestion of a Great Lakes modification of secondary low level 
trough late in the day, guidance has backed off a bit on gust 
magnitude during the day, but would suspect some gusts to 30 to 
35 mph would be possible. A few gusts approaching 40 mph appear 
most likely near immediate Lake Michigan shoreline. Given cold 
advection, temperatures are not likely to move much from morning
levels with near steady temps in the 50s expected.

No major changes have been made to the long term forecast as below 
normal temperatures will continue through the weekend. Low 
temperatures in the 30s are still on track with a potential of 
patchy frost. The Friday night potential remains somewhat more 
uncertain as some lingering lake effect clouds could persist 
across the west, while winds may not full decouple across the 
east. Saturday night still appears to be best chance of patchy 
frost depending on extent of southwest return flow with 
departing high pressure.

Mid/upper level flow is still progged to rapidly deamplify early 
next week which will result in conditions warming to above normal 
levels into the lower 70s toward the end of the period.
